rebuilds.why: Execution on 'That he stayed about ten minutes with their father' placed 'sat about ten minutes' at line 5, inside the 5-8 window; it is at line 4, outside it. Rewrote that execution with the true line and, because the detail is outside the window, retagged it from en-within-span-wrong-element to en-wrong-scope-retrieval (the within-span tag asserts the detail is inside the window). Nothing else changed.

stem.text: The Bennet daughters did not meet Mr Bingley when he called at their house. Read lines 5 to 8. What were they able to find out about him?

options.value: That he was cheerful and talked to everybody.
options.execution: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at lines 36 and 37, at the ball — true, and a different part of the passage. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: That he had ten thousand pounds a year.
options.execution: Ten thousand a year is Mr Darcy's, at line 29, carried across to Mr Bingley. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.
That he stayed about ten minutes with their father.
options.execution: The ten-minute visit is at line 4, just before the window opens at line 5. It is true, and it is what happened in Mr Bennet's library, not what the daughters found out from the upper window at lines 7 and 8.

options.value: That he liked the big house he had taken.
options.execution: Nothing says he liked the house; taking it makes it sound like something they could have learned.

rebuilds.why: Execution on 'A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet' invented an interval ('weeks after this visit') and put the dancing at lines 36 to 41. Rewrote it: his dance with the eldest Miss Bennet is at lines 60 and 61, a later scene, and the passage gives no interval. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Mr Bingley hoped for something on this visit that he did not get. Read lines 5 to 6. What was it?

options.value: A book from Mr Bennet's library.
options.execution: The library is line 5 and true, and no book is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

options.value: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.
A chance to invite the Bennets to dinner at his own house.
options.execution: It reverses who invites whom: line 9 has the invitation going FROM the Bennets.

options.value: A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
options.execution: The black horse at line 8 is a thing the ladies saw, turned into something he wanted. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.

options.value: A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet.
options.execution: His dance with the eldest Miss Bennet is at lines 60 and 61, at the assembly, a later scene in the passage, and it is something he did get. On this visit, lines 5 and 6 give what he hoped for: a sight of the young ladies.

rebuilds.why: hintCore quoted the answer clause 'obliged to be in town', which the key paraphrases (R572). Replaced it with a move that sends the child to the answer itself and away from Lady Lucas's later guess, without quoting or paraphrasing the key. Removed the quote declaration the old hint needed; the walkScript does not quote that phrase.

stem.text: Mr Bingley said no to the Bennets' dinner. Read lines 9 to 12. What reason did his answer give?

options.value: He had promised to dine with Lady Lucas instead.
options.execution: Lady Lucas is at line 15 and says nothing about dining; the answer names no rival engagement at all.

options.value: He did not want to meet the Bennet daughters.
options.execution: A wish to avoid the daughters is supplied; lines 5 and 6 have him hoping to see them.

options.value: He was busy planning the courses for a dinner of his own.
options.execution: The planning of courses at lines 9 and 10 is MRS BENNET'S, carried across to him.

options.value: He had to be in London the next day.
He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.
options.execution: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. In the window, line 11 answers the stem: 'which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to'.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Read only what his answer says. Leave out what other people guess later.

rebuilds.why: Option 'They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley' is true of lines 34 and 35 as an OUTCOME of the change (his face found forbidding, him unworthy to be compared with his friend); its execution said only that line 30 contradicts it, and the tag did not name the mistake. Retagged to en-chronology-collapse (a later event in the passage given as the cause of an earlier one) and rewrote the execution to say the verdict on his looks follows the turn at lines 31 and 32. Option value, key and explanation unchanged.

stem.text: Halfway through the evening, people changed their minds about Mr Darcy. Read lines 30 to 35. What changed them?

options.value: They found out that he was not really rich after all.
options.execution: Nothing says the money was doubted; line 33 still calls the estate large.

options.value: They decided he was less good-looking than Mr Bingley.
options.execution: Lines 34 and 35 do have the room find his face forbidding and him unworthy to be compared with Mr Bingley. That verdict comes after his manners turned the tide at lines 31 and 32, so the child gives the result of the change as its cause.

options.value: The way he behaved, as if he were better than everyone there.
He complained that the ball had ended too early.
options.execution: Complaining that the ball closed early is Mr Bingley at line 37, transferred to Mr Darcy. In the window, line 31 answers the stem: 'with great admiration for about half the evening, till'.

options.value: Everybody disliked him from the moment he walked in.
options.execution: 'From the moment he walked in' overstates: line 30 has him admired for half the evening.

rebuilds.why: hintCore offered a binary ('the writer's own, or the room's?') whose second half is the key (R572). Replaced it with a move: notice how certain the sentences are, then ask what they rest on. The hold's second fault (the 'said nothing to anybody all evening' option tagged en-wrong-scope-retrieval) is already repaired on the stored row, which carries en-contradicted-by-the-text with an execution citing 'speaking occasionally' (line 41) 'to one of his own party' (line 42); checked against the passage and left as it is.

stem.text: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

quotes.text: His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
options.execution: 'Really was the worst man alive' takes the room's verdict as the writer's own finding.

options.value: They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
options.execution: A motive is supplied for the writer; the shortness is doing the room's certainty, not his.

options.value: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
options.execution: Takes 'his character was decided' as Mr Darcy deciding something. NOTE REPAIRED 2026-08-16 (delivery 52): 'decided' meaning MADE A DECISION is the sense that arrives first, not 'the other sense' — the passage's sense, settled and no longer open to question, is the rarer one. The error is a dominant sense displacing a rarer one. Tag grandfathered; the note is not.

options.value: They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.
options.execution: Lines 41 and 42 have Mr Darcy speaking occasionally to one of his own party, so the passage states the contrary. The child takes his coldness to mean total silence and misses what the short, sure sentences do.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Notice how certain these short sentences are. Then ask what they are based on.

rebuilds.why: hintCore quoted the key's own phrase 'one of her daughters' (R572). Replaced it with a move (read on from line 44 for what made her dislike sharper) and removed the quote declaration only that hint used; the walkScript's declared quotation 'slighted one of her daughters' stays. Also corrected a false line number in the en-cause-agent-swap execution: Mr Bingley's dancing with the eldest daughter is lines 60 and 61, not line 63.

stem.text: Mrs Bennet disliked Mr Darcy more strongly than anybody else in the room did. Read lines 44 to 46. What made her feeling so strong?

options.value: He had been rude about one of her daughters.
He would not let anyone introduce him to her.
options.execution: Declining to be introduced is line 40, and it is to any other LADY, not to Mrs Bennet in particular. In the window, line 44 answers the stem: 'Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet'.

options.value: He had told Mr Bennet that he did not like the neighbourhood.
options.execution: Mr Bennet is not at the ball at all in this passage, and no such remark is made.

options.value: Mr Bingley had chosen to dance with her eldest daughter.
options.execution: The cause is moved to Mr Bingley's dancing with the eldest daughter at lines 60 and 61; lines 45 and 46 name the slight as the reason.

options.value: He was the proudest man in the world, and she hated proud people.
options.execution: The child takes line 42's 'the proudest ... man in the world' and adds a general reason, a dislike of proud people, that the passage never gives Mrs Bennet. Lines 45 and 46 give her own reason: he had slighted one of her daughters.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Read on from line 44. Find what made her dislike sharper than everyone else's.

rebuilds.why: hintCore asked the child to define 'scarcity of gentlemen', whose definition is the key (R572). Replaced it with a move: find the word in line 47 that says she had no choice (obliged) and ask what forced her. Removed the quote declaration only that hint used; the walkScript's declared quotation stays.

stem.text: Elizabeth had to sit down for two dances. Read lines 47 to 48. Why?

options.value: She did not feel like dancing that evening.
options.execution: A wish not to dance is supplied; line 47 says she was OBLIGED to sit down.

options.value: Mr Darcy had refused to dance with her.
options.execution: Line 47 has Elizabeth already sitting down because there were too few gentlemen. Mr Darcy's refusal comes at lines 65 to 67, while she is sitting, so the child gives a later event as the cause of an earlier one.

options.value: She wanted to listen to Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley talking.
options.execution: A motive is supplied; line 48 has the overhearing happen because he stood near enough, not because she arranged it.

options.value: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.
Her eldest sister was dancing with Mr Bingley.
options.execution: Her eldest sister dancing with Mr Bingley is line 60, true, and not the reason line 47 gives.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Find the word in line 47 that says she had no choice. What forced her?

quotes.text: obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit down

rebuilds.why: walkScript ended 'The room hears nothing of this', which the passage never says (line 48 says only that Mr Darcy stood near enough for Elizabeth to overhear). Removed that sentence; the rest of the walk is unchanged.

stem.text: Elizabeth hears Mr Darcy's words herself. A friend does not tell her later. Read lines 47 to 50. Why is that a good choice?

options.value: It shows that Elizabeth enjoyed listening in on other people.
options.execution: A taste for listening in is supplied; line 48 has him standing near enough for her to overhear.

options.value: It shows that the room had almost emptied by then.
options.execution: An empty room is not stated; line 49 has Mr Bingley coming from the dance, so it is in progress.

options.value: The reader hears the unkind words at the very moment Elizabeth does.
Mr Bingley had planned for her to hear his kind words about her.
options.execution: The planning is given to Mr Bingley, and the words Elizabeth hears are Mr Darcy's, not his.

options.value: It shows that Mr Darcy was speaking loudly to the whole room.
options.execution: Lines 48 and 49 have Elizabeth overhear a conversation between Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley, because Mr Darcy was standing near her. The child turns overhearing into Mr Darcy speaking loudly to everyone, which those lines contradict.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Line 48 puts him 'near enough for her to overhear'. So the words come in his voice. You hear them as Elizabeth does.

rebuilds.why: walkScript ended 'Putting up with things is the other sense', but putting up with things is the meaning of the different word tolerant, not a sense of 'tolerable' (as the row's own en-vocab-form-lookalike execution says). Replaced that sentence so it says the meaning belongs to a different word. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Read lines 65 to 67. Mr Darcy says Elizabeth 'is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me'. What does 'tolerable' mean here?

options.value: Kind, and easy to get along with.
options.execution: Kind and easy to get along with is no meaning of 'tolerable'. The child guesses a word about temperament, where line 66 uses it about how Elizabeth looks: only just good enough.

options.value: Good at putting up with things without complaining.
options.execution: Putting up with things without complaining is the meaning of 'tolerant', a different word the target resembles in form. The child has misidentified the word; line 66 uses 'tolerable' about how Elizabeth looks.

options.value: Only just good enough to look at.
Very good-looking, so he is paying her a compliment.
options.execution: Lines 66 and 67 say at once that she is 'not handsome enough to tempt me', which states the contrary of very good-looking. The child reads 'tolerable' as praise and does not read on to the rest of the sentence.

options.value: Too proud to dance with anybody.
options.execution: The pride belongs to Mr Darcy, who at line 32 is found to be proud and above his company. The child moves it onto Elizabeth, whom the word 'tolerable' describes at line 66.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Read on from 'tolerable' in line 66. It is 'but not handsome enough to tempt me'. So it means only just good enough. Putting up with things belongs to a different word, tolerant.

rebuilds.why: The key ('never whether the writer agrees') was not the only defensible answer: the writer characterises Mr Bingley directly at lines 24 and 25 and Elizabeth at lines 72 and 73, which supported the distractor 'We are told what the writer thinks'. No small repair fixes a false whole-passage premise, so the question is REWRITTEN on the same passage, same questionType (en-comp-technique) and same tier (4), narrowed to Mr Darcy, whose character the passage gives only through the room (lines 29 to 35, 42 to 46) and then his own overheard words (lines 53 to 56, 60 to 61, 65 to 69). techniqueKey and answerShape changed to match. New key: the room's verdict comes first, then his own words. Distractors: only Elizabeth's view (kept, en-extreme-option-pull, execution redrafted for the new stem); the writer says he is kind underneath (en-plausible-not-stated: a reader who knows the novel may supply it, no line gives it); he never speaks (en-contradicted-by-the-text: lines 53 to 69). hintCore rewritten as a move, and it no longer calls the writer 'he'. walkScript rewritten to match. lineRefs stay empty (whole passage).

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How do we learn what Mr Darcy is like?

options.value: The writer tells us herself that he is kind under all his pride.
options.execution: No line says Mr Darcy is kind underneath. A reader who knows how the story ends may supply it, but this passage gives only his pride and his rude words at lines 53 to 56 and 65 to 69.

options.value: He never speaks, so we have only the room's word for what he is like.
options.execution: Lines 53 to 56 and 65 to 69 give Mr Darcy's own words to Mr Bingley, so the passage states the contrary. The child remembers the room's verdict at lines 42 and 43 and forgets the talk Elizabeth overhears.

options.value: We are given only Elizabeth's view, and no other opinion is ever allowed.
options.execution: Elizabeth's feelings about him appear only at lines 70 and 71. Before that come the room's opinion at lines 29 to 43, Mrs Bennet's at lines 44 to 46, and his own words at lines 53 to 69, so 'only' claims far too much.

options.value: We hear the room's verdict on him first, and then his own words.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Find each place where we learn about him. Ask who is speaking each time.
explanationPatch.walkScript: Lines 29 to 35 give what the gentlemen and the ladies think of him. Lines 42 to 46 give the room's verdict and Mrs Bennet's. Then lines 53 to 69 let us hear his own words to Mr Bingley. So the room speaks first, and then we hear him.

rebuilds.why: Execution on 'The green squares of the fields' said they are what the travellers pass over; line 3 has the hill rising over the fields. Rewrote the execution to say so. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 4. What does Dr Mortimer point out of the window?

options.value: The first sight of the moor itself.
The green squares of the fields.
options.execution: True at line 3, where the far hill rises over the fields. Dr Mortimer points out the moor itself at lines 1 and 2, not the fields in front of it.

options.value: The small station where they get down.
options.execution: True at line 11, outside this window; lines 1 to 4 have them still on the train.

options.value: The road that runs up to the Hall.
options.execution: They are bound for the Hall; lines 1 to 4 never mention a road.

rebuilds.why: hintCore 'Two of these sit in one window only' was false (only the 'eyes fixed' option sits in one window). Replaced it with a move: read each window, then say what is different. The lamps option's execution carried a false appended clause ('line 9 answers the stem'); removed it, and gave the lamps lines as 69 to 71. Also corrected the en-chronology-collapse execution's arithmetic: line 45 is thirty-six lines after line 9, not thirty-five.

stem.text: Look at lines 5 to 10 and 45 to 46. What has changed in Sir Henry?

options.value: His eyes were fixed upon it, and his face was eager to see it.
options.execution: Reuses lines 5 and 6, and both halves come from the first window alone.

options.value: He is a brave comrade at first, but the moor has silenced him.
He falls silent first, but Watson had judged him brave.
options.execution: Line 45 comes thirty-six lines after line 9, so this turns the order round.

options.value: He talks of electric lamps, and then he says nothing more.
options.execution: True at lines 69 to 71, outside both windows; neither window has him speak at all.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Read the first window, then the second. What is different about him?

rebuilds.why: hintCore 'Ask what does not belong in a sweet, simple spot' restated the key almost word for word (R572). Replaced it with a move: find the word that says Watson was surprised (line 13) and read either side of it. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 11 to 16. Why does Watson call the sight a surprising one?

options.value: They leaned on their rifles and glanced keenly at him.
options.execution: Reuses lines 14 and 15 and describes the men rather than saying what is odd.

options.value: A wagonette and a pair of cobs waited outside.
options.execution: True at line 12, and it is what was expected there rather than what was not.

options.value: Armed men do not belong in a sweet and simple spot.
The little station was too small for so many people.
options.execution: A likely enough complaint; lines 11 to 16 never say it.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Find the word that says Watson was surprised. Read what comes either side of it.

rebuilds.why: Execution on 'Was covered over by a skirt' opened 'The commonest everyday sense of the word', which is false of 'skirted' and describes en-vocab-dominant-sense, not its tag en-vocab-built-from-parts. Rewrote it to describe the built-from-parts mistake (the noun skirt read inside the verb) and dropped the retag history note that contradicted the first sentence. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 21 to 29. What does 'skirted' on line 24 mean here?

options.value: Went along the edge of it.
Was covered over by a skirt.
options.execution: The child finds the noun skirt inside skirted and adds the parts up to a covering. The parts are real, but the sum is not this word. Line 24 has them skirting a noisy stream, going along beside it.

options.value: Kept a long way clear of.
options.execution: A real sense of the word; line 26 has road and stream wind up together.

options.value: Passed over a narrow granite bridge.
options.execution: True at line 24, and it is the other thing they did rather than the meaning.

rebuilds.why: The stem asked 'What has the moor got in it besides stone?' while the key and the executions answer what chills Sir Henry, over lines 40 to 46. Fixed the STEM to the question the key answers (what has chilled him, as even he falls silent at line 45) and widened the window and lineRefs to 40 to 46, which the executions already cite. Key, options, tags and executions unchanged. Added one walkScript sentence for line 45, now inside the window.

stem.text: Look at lines 40 to 46. Even Sir Henry falls silent. What has chilled him?

options.value: He pulled his overcoat more closely round him.
options.execution: Reuses line 46 and names what he did rather than why he did it.

options.value: The moor was mottled with gnarled and craggy cairns.
options.execution: True at line 41, and it is the look of the place rather than what chills him.

options.value: The bare moor and the hidden man together chill him.
He is beginning to wish he had never come home.
options.execution: A plausible thought for him here; lines 40 to 46 never give it.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Line 40 has the huge expanse of the moor rise in front of them. Lines 42 and 43 put the escaped man out there, lurking like a beast. Line 44 says it needed but this to complete the grim feeling. At line 45 even Baskerville fell silent.

rebuilds.why: Key 'The gold and the green give way to bare stone' misstated lines 47 to 51 (no green is given for the country behind; the slopes ahead are russet and olive and sprinkled with boulders, not bare stone). Rewrote the key to what lines 47 to 50 say: the fertile country is left behind and the road ahead grows bleaker and wilder. The hint ('The question asks about ahead') pulled against a behind-to-ahead key; replaced it with a move: a change needs a before and an after. Distractors, tags, executions and walkScript unchanged and checked against the new key, except one gate-forced wording: the child-facing gate holds 'high' in an option with no sentence to fix its sense (subject-matter), so 'Two high, narrow towers' became 'Two tall, narrow towers'; the option still restates line 54 and keeps its tag and execution.

stem.text: Look at lines 47 to 55. How does the land change as they drive on?

options.value: They were driving down towards the fertile country.
options.execution: Line 47 says they had left the fertile country behind and beneath them.

options.value: The low sun turned the streams to threads of gold.
options.execution: Reuses line 48 and describes what they look back at rather than the change.

options.value: Two tall, narrow towers rose over the trees.
options.execution: True at line 54, and it is what they arrive at rather than how the land changed.

options.value: They leave fertile farmland behind for bleaker, wilder country ahead.

explanationPatch.hintCore: A change needs a before and an after. Find both in these lines.

rebuilds.why: Execution on 'Night had fallen before they reached it' cited line 57 for the fading light; 'fading light' is line 73 and line 57 says nothing of light. Rewrote it with the true line. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 61 to 67. What does the writer use to make the drive feel closed in?

options.value: The house glimmered like a ghost at the far end.
options.execution: Reuses lines 63 and 64, and that image works by distance rather than by closeness.

options.value: The old trees arching right over their heads.
The wheels were hushed among the fallen leaves.
options.execution: True at line 61, and it is a sound rather than anything that closes them in.

options.value: Night had fallen before they reached it.
options.execution: A dark drive invites it, but no line says night had fallen. At line 73 Watson still sees the house in the fading light.

rebuilds.why: walkScript said the hill at line 4 is melancholy 'before anyone has said a word', but Dr Mortimer speaks at lines 1 and 2; and it said Nature 'throws at them' where line 28 has 'throw before the carriage'. Removed the false clause, and made the line 27 sentence say the rotting plants are thrown before the carriage. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How does Watson write about the moor?

options.value: He tells us the hills were jagged, and the wind was very cold.
options.execution: Reuses lines 20 and 41 and reports two details rather than anything the telling does.

options.value: The moor is calm by day, but it turns cruel after dark.
options.execution: A tidy shape the passage never carries: line 4 is grim in broad daylight.

options.value: He is afraid of the moor, so he keeps his eyes on the road.
options.execution: A plausible reason to look away; nowhere does he say he looked away from it.

options.value: He writes a still moor, but he gives it a mind of its own.

explanationPatch.walkScript: At line 4 the far-off hill is melancholy. At line 8 the moor is forbidding, and at line 20 the hills are sinister. At line 27 the rotting plants become sad gifts that Nature throws before the carriage.

rebuilds.why: walkScript put 'She said it on Monday' at line 13; it is line 12, and line 13 is that the butterflies were still asleep on Monday. Rewrote the walk with the true lines. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 12 to 16. How does Dilan deal with Miss Deller’s instruction?

options.value: Miss Deller said nobody was to open the net except her.
options.execution: Reuses line 12 and repeats her rather than saying what he does.

options.value: Miss Deller had said that anybody could open the net.
options.execution: Line 12 turns on nobody, and this option drops it.

options.value: He remembers that Marnie was against the water fountain.
options.execution: True at lines 15 and 16, and it is about Marnie rather than the rule.

options.value: He treats it as out of date, a Monday rule on a Thursday.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Line 12 says nobody was to open the net except her. The same line says she said it on Monday. Line 13 says they were all still asleep then. Line 14 says the instruction is out of date.

rebuilds.why: walkScript 'Line 27 says that is what half past two is like' misreported lines 26 and 27, which say the screaming is just what Reception is like at half past two. Rewrote that sentence. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 25 to 28. What does Dilan say about Reception?

options.value: That seven of the butterflies are back.
options.execution: True at line 28, and it is about the butterflies.

options.value: They had to sit down and have a drink of water.
options.execution: True at line 25, and it belongs to Miss Deller, not Reception.

options.value: They are fine, and the screaming is just what Reception is like.
Their teacher took the whole class outside.
options.execution: Screaming invites a teacher acting; no line gives one.

explanationPatch.walkScript: Line 26 says Reception are fine. Line 26 says some of them are screaming. Lines 26 and 27 say that is just what Reception is like at half past two.
